strengths: REFINE addresses a practical active-learning problem: selection strategies perform differently across datasets, backbones, and labeling budgets. Its progressive union filtering is a simple, modular contribution that can incorporate existing batch-selection methods without learning a strategy-selection policy.

The empirical evaluation is substantial within frozen-feature classification: three foundation models, five main evaluation datasets separate from CIFAR-10 used for hyperparameter selection, and ten trials per configuration. REFINE achieves aggregate AULC win rates of 80% against UHerding and 85% against BAIT, and 98–100% against the evaluated ensemble methods.

The preprocessing ablations provide useful evidence beyond the full system. Figure 5 reports improvements for all six tested downstream selectors across DINOv2 and DINOv3, including 0.7–1.2% AULC improvements for the already strong UHerding. Improving random sampling from the filtered pool supports the claim that filtering changes candidate quality.

The manuscript clearly explains the algorithm and its design choices, supplies extensive supplementary learning curves, and acknowledges a concrete failure case on Dopanim with CLIP. The audio experiment also explores transfer to Coreset, which is outside the filtering ensemble.
weaknesses: Theorem 3 is not established by its proof. Appendix A replaces the expected average of a randomly sized selected pool with the ratio of expected weighted value to expected pool size. In general, E[sum_x V(x)I_x / sum_x I_x] is not equal to sum_x V(x)P_x / sum_x P_x. Selection dependencies and random pool size therefore cannot be discarded. The theorem also blurs an expected guarantee with monotonicity of realized pools. This undermines a prominently claimed theoretical contribution.

The theoretical assumptions provide limited support for actual model improvement. Theorem 3 requires every strategy to weakly preserve the ordering of every pair of instances by a shared true value, which is much stronger than a heuristic being useful on average and sits uneasily with the motivation of complementary, sometimes failing strategies. Theorem 2 defines uninformative instances through uniformly low selection probability across all rounds; it does not establish that removed instances have low downstream learning utility.

The distinctive benefit of repeated heterogeneous filtering is not fully isolated. Table 2 evaluates filtering depth with random downstream selection on two datasets, but does not compare the complete REFINE pipeline against one-round union filtering followed by the same UHerding selector across the main benchmark. Repeated filtering with only the strongest constituent is also missing. These controls matter because much of the improvement may come from candidate preselection rather than progressive combination itself.

Computational practicality remains unquantified. With eight strategies, five rounds, and ten batches per strategy, the default procedure invokes constituent selectors 400 times per AL cycle before final selection. Shrinking pools can reduce this cost substantially, but there are no measured runtimes, peak-memory results, or accuracy–compute comparisons. Consequently, the claimed practical trade-off cannot be assessed.

Statistical and reproduction details are incomplete. Standard errors are explicitly omitted, while pooled win rates obscure dataset-specific uncertainty and effect sizes. The manuscript provides no usable implementation link, and does not fully specify constituent-strategy settings, the UHerding kernel/uncertainty configuration, or how undersized subsamples are handled. All vision experiments train only a linear head, which also limits the scope of the broader deep-active-learning claims.

Overall, the broad empirical gains make this a credible and potentially useful contribution. However, the unsupported central guarantee and incomplete attribution and cost evidence leave the recommendation at the decision boundary.

strengths: REFINE offers a useful, modular contribution to batch active learning: repeatedly unioning selections from complementary strategies refines the candidate pool before final coverage-based selection. The novelty is primarily this filtering mechanism, which can also improve existing acquisition workflows.

The empirical support is substantial within frozen-feature classification: five evaluation datasets beyond CIFAR-10 used for hyperparameter selection, three vision backbones, and ten trials. REFINE achieves aggregate AULC win rates of 80% against UHerding and 85% against BAIT, and 98–100% against the evaluated ensemble methods (Figures 2 and 4).

The ablations provide evidence that filtering itself contributes. Figure 5 reports improvements of 0.7–5.4% in AULC across downstream selectors, including random sampling. The two-strategy experiment and the supplementary Coreset audio experiment further support modularity and complementarity.

The algorithm is clearly described, and the manuscript acknowledges ensemble-composition sensitivity and the Dopanim/CLIP failure case. Overall, the supported empirical contribution favors acceptance despite the theoretical and practical reservations below.

In general, an expectation of a ratio does not equal a ratio of expectations. Moreover, the theorem displays monotonicity for realized pool averages, which random subsampling does not guarantee. This is a substantive correctness issue in the claimed theoretical contribution, although it does not invalidate the experimental results.

The theoretical interpretation is stronger than the assumptions support. Theorem 3 requires every strategy to respect the same pairwise ordering of true instance value, substantially stronger than merely being a useful heuristic. Theorem 2 defines uninformative instances through persistently low selection probability across all rounds, rather than demonstrating low downstream utility. These results therefore offer limited justification for the broader claim that filtering removes genuinely uninformative data.

Computational practicality is insufficiently quantified. With eight strategies, five rounds, and ten batches per strategy, the default configuration makes 400 strategy calls per acquisition cycle before final selection. Smaller pools may reduce their cost, but no measured runtime, peak memory, or accuracy-versus-compute comparison establishes the proposed trade-off. Table 2 already shows substantial gains with one filtering round, making this comparison particularly relevant.

Aggregate win rates establish consistency but obscure effect sizes and variation across tasks. Standard errors are explicitly omitted, and numerical per-dataset AULC differences with uncertainty are absent. The filtering ablations also do not directly establish how much full REFINE gains over a single-round union followed by the same final selector.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the code reference is an 'anonymous' placeholder, baseline-specific settings are not fully documented, and the minimum-pool safeguard is absent from Algorithm 1. Enforcing |C_R| >= b alone also does not ensure intermediate subsamples contain b candidates when alpha < 1. Finally, the image experiments use frozen backbones and linear heads, so broader claims about deep active learning should be scoped to the demonstrated setting.

strengths: REFINE addresses a relevant practical problem: individual active-learning strategies vary in effectiveness across datasets, backbones, and labeling budgets. Repeatedly unioning their selections before final acquisition is a simple, modular contribution that accommodates existing batch strategies.

The reported empirical results are strong: across five evaluation datasets, three backbones, and ten trials, REFINE wins 85% of comparisons against BAIT and 80% against UHerding, and 97–100% against the ensemble baselines. Complete learning curves and uncertainty bands provide useful supporting evidence.

The ablations meaningfully separate filtering from final acquisition. Random sampling benefits from filtered pools, and Figure 5 reports improvements across several downstream strategies. The audio experiment additionally evaluates Coreset, which is outside the filtering ensemble.

The supplement substantially broadens evaluation through class imbalance, medical images, partial backbone fine-tuning, batch-size variation, and weak ensemble members. These experiments strengthen the contribution beyond frozen-feature classification on standard benchmarks.
weaknesses: A consequential inconsistency separates Algorithm 1 from the reported pool sizes. Each round unions M × J batches of b instances, so |Cr| ≤ MJb. With eight strategies, J = 10, and CIFAR-10's b = 10, every filtered pool contains at most 800 instances, approximately 1.6% of the roughly 50,000-instance unlabeled pool. Table 4 instead reports 16.3% after round 1 and 5.2% after round 5. CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet also exceed their corresponding bounds. An undocumented subsampling protocol or different batch construction could explain this, but the manuscript does not establish which algorithm produced the experiments.

Theorem 3 is not established by its proof. Appendix A replaces the average over a random, variable-size pool with a ratio of expected sums: sum_x V(x)Pr(x) / sum_x Pr(x). This generally differs from the expectation of the pool average. Moreover, the stated inequalities concern realized pool averages, which stochastic filtering need not preserve monotonically. The assumption that every strategy orders selection probabilities consistently with the same true value is also substantially stronger than the motivating claim that strategies capture complementary, sometimes unreliable notions of value.

The computational advantage remains incompletely supported. Table 3 reports approximately ten minutes of sequential acquisition, exceeding AutoAL's reported acquisition times at both evaluated cycles. Parallel timings are projections based on assumed parallel fractions and overheads, rather than measurements. No comprehensive comparison with individual strategies or measured peak-memory results establishes the claimed practical efficiency.

Reproducibility details are insufficient to resolve the main implementation uncertainty. The implementation-link sentence is empty, baseline-specific configurations are not adequately documented, and the procedure enforcing the minimum candidate-pool size is unspecified. The protocol states 20 cycles with Snacks batches of 20, whereas the complete learning curves end near 200 labels, adding another unexplained discrepancy.

The broad empirical gains provide a worthwhile case for the method, but the algorithm–measurement inconsistency and invalid central theoretical argument currently outweigh those merits. These concerns affect confidence in what was evaluated and what is guaranteed; they are more substantial than presentation refinements.

strengths: REFINE offers a simple, useful contribution to batch active learning: repeatedly unioning selections from complementary strategies produces a candidate pool that can support different downstream acquisition methods. Its modularity and lack of an additional learned controller are practical advantages.

The empirical evidence is substantial: six image datasets, three foundation models, and ten trials, with CIFAR-10 reserved for hyperparameter selection in the main comparisons. Reported AULC win rates reach 85% against BAIT, 80% against UHerding, and 97–100% against competing ensemble methods. The learning curves support meaningful improvements, particularly at smaller annotation budgets.

The ablations provide evidence that filtering itself contributes beyond the final UHerding selector. Random sampling and several individual strategies improve on filtered pools; the Margin–TypiClust experiment illustrates complementary acquisition behavior. The audio experiment additionally evaluates Coreset, which is outside the filtering ensemble.

The supplementary evaluation meaningfully broadens support through class imbalance, medical imagery, partial backbone fine-tuning, batch-size variation, and weak ensemble members. The manuscript also acknowledges dependence on ensemble composition and the failure to dominate on Dopanim with CLIP.
weaknesses: Theorem 3 is not established by its proof. Appendix A equates the average of a randomly selected pool with a ratio weighted by marginal inclusion probabilities. Because the union's cardinality is random, the expectation of its average generally differs from the ratio of expected value-sum to expected cardinality. Furthermore, the displayed guarantee concerns realized pool averages, whereas an expectation over filtering randomness would require a different statement. This undermines the claimed monotonic improvement guarantee, although it does not invalidate the empirical gains.

The reported pool sizes conflict with Algorithm 1 under the stated settings. Each round unions M×J batches of size b, so |C_r|≤MJb. With eight strategies, J=10, and CIFAR-10's b=10, at most 800 candidates can survive, approximately 1.6% of its roughly 50,000-instance pool. Table 4 instead reports 16.3% after round one and 5.2% after round five. An unreported initial pool cap or different settings could explain this, but the discrepancy leaves the implemented filtering protocol and scalability evidence unclear.

The theoretical connection to actual annotation utility is limited even apart from the proof error. Theorem 2 defines uninformative instances through persistently low selection probabilities, rather than low contribution to generalization. Theorem 3 assumes every strategy orders every pair consistently with a common true value—substantially stronger than merely having useful, complementary heuristics. These results do not justify the broader claims of reliably removing genuinely uninformative examples.

The computational tradeoff is incompletely isolated. The default configuration makes 400 constituent acquisition calls per cycle before final selection. Table 3 reports roughly ten minutes of sequential acquisition, while parallel timings are projections rather than measurements. Table 2 shows that one filtering round already supplies much of the improvement; a compute-matched comparison with simpler repeated-sampling or single-round ensemble alternatives would better establish the value of progressive refinement.

Overall, the broad empirical improvements and reusable design make this a credible contribution. However, the invalid monotonicity argument and concrete mismatch between the algorithm and reported pool sizes are substantive unresolved issues. Together they place the present manuscript at the acceptance boundary rather than supporting a clear acceptance recommendation.
